title: Cosmological constraints and standard sirens forecasts for non-dynamical dark energy in Horndeski gravity
comment: 23 pages, 19 figures, 2 tables
summary: We investigate an analytically tractable sector of the Extended Cuscuton model, a non-dynamical dark-energy realization within the framework of viable Horndeski gravity. We focus on four benchmark submodels and constrain them with current background probes, namely cosmic chronometers, Type-Ia supernovae, and BAO, while imposing theoretical viability, Lunar Laser Ranging, and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis bounds. We then forecast third-generation bright-standard-siren constraints with Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer networks, considering prompt-emission, afterglow, and kilonova counterparts. Current data already restrict the viable parameter space to small departures from $Λ$CDM and do not remove the calibration-driven offset between the CC+SN and CC+BAO determinations of $H_0$. In principle, future bright sirens substantially sharpen the constraints, especially for kilonova catalogues and extended detector networks. Across the forecast configurations, the relative uncertainty on $H_0$ remains below $13.18\%$ and can reach $0.21\%$ in the most constraining cases, while $Ω_Λ$ is recovered at the percent level in the best cases. These results show that third-generation standard sirens can provide a precise complementary test of non-dynamical dark energy beyond $Λ$CDM.

AI.tldr: The paper investigates an analytically tractable sector of the Extended Cuscuton model, a non-dynamical dark-energy realization in Horndeski gravity, constraining four benchmark submodels with current background probes (cosmic chronometers, Type-Ia supernovae, BAO) and theoretical/observational bounds, then forecasting third-generation bright-standard-siren constraints using Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer. Current data restrict parameter space to small deviations from ΛCDM without resolving the H0 tension between CC+SN and CC+BAO, while future bright sirens (especially kilonova catalogues and extended networks) could sharply improve constraints, with H0 uncertainty between 0.21% and 13.18% and ΩΛ recovered at percent level in best cases.
AI.motivation: To test whether non-dynamical dark-energy models beyond ΛCDM, specifically the Extended Cuscuton model within Horndeski gravity, are viable given current cosmological data and whether future third-generation gravitational-wave standard sirens can provide precise complementary constraints on such models.
AI.method: The authors focus on four benchmark submodels of the analytically tractable Extended Cuscuton sector. They constrain these models using current background probes (cosmic chronometers, Type-Ia supernovae, BAO) while imposing theoretical viability, Lunar Laser Ranging, and Big Bang Nucleosynthesis bounds. They then perform forecasts for third-generation bright-standard-siren constraints from Einstein Telescope and Cosmic Explorer networks, considering prompt-emission, afterglow, and kilonova electromagnetic counterparts.
AI.result: Current data restrict the viable parameter space to small departures from ΛCDM and do not remove the calibration-driven offset between CC+SN and CC+BAO H0 determinations. Future bright sirens substantially sharpen constraints, especially for kilonova catalogues and extended detector networks. Across forecast configurations, the relative uncertainty on H0 remains below 13.18% and can reach 0.21% in the most constraining cases, with ΩΛ recovered at the percent level in the best cases.
AI.conclusion: Third-generation standard sirens can provide a precise complementary test of non-dynamical dark energy beyond ΛCDM, demonstrating strong potential to sharpen constraints on the Extended Cuscuton model and potentially shed light on persisting cosmological tensions.

title: Revisiting the equation of state of dark energy from DESI BAO with SNe Ia and CMB
comment: 16 pages, 3 figures, 6 tabels
summary: The Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) measurements of baryon acoustic oscillations (BAO) have recently shown a mild preference for dynamical dark energy over the standard $\rm Λ$CDM model. In this paper, we analyze the $w_0w_a$CDM model using DESI BAO DR2, Pantheon+ SNe Ia, and Planck 2018 CMB distance prior data. To examine how different parts of the data affect the apparent deviation from $\rm Λ$CDM, we adopt two complementary redshift-cut strategies, dividing the dataset into $z<z_{\rm cut}$ and $z>z_{\rm cut}$ subsamples. We find that the most noticeable shifts occur when BAO and SNe Ia data in the redshift range $z\sim0.4$--$0.8$ are included, reaching a significance of about $\sim2σ$. Within this framework, the inclusion of higher-redshift measurements progressively weakens this deviation and brings the constraints closer to the $\rm Λ$CDM expectation. Moreover, the information criteria show no statistically significant preference between the $w_0w_a$CDM and $\rm Λ$CDM models, while the Bayesian information criterion consistently favors the $\rm Λ$CDM model. In addition, a parameter-shift consistency test reveals no statistically significant tension between complementary redshift subsamples. Within the DESI BAO DR2, Pantheon+, and CMB distance prior framework adopted here, these results do not provide statistically robust evidence favoring the $w_0w_a$CDM model over $\rm Λ$CDM. They instead indicate that the apparent parameter shifts under different redshift cuts may be affected by statistical fluctuations and by the limited precision and number of datapoints in the current subsamples. Our analysis provides a complementary redshift-dependent diagnostic for assessing how the inferred cosmological constraints vary under different redshift selections.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes the w0waCDM dark energy model using DESI BAO DR2, Pantheon+ SNe Ia, and Planck 2018 CMB distance prior data to investigate the mild preference for dynamical dark energy over ΛCDM. Using redshift-cut strategies, the authors find that apparent deviations from ΛCDM, reaching ~2σ, are driven primarily by data in the z~0.4–0.8 range, but higher-redshift data weaken this preference. Statistical tests show no robust evidence favoring w0waCDM over ΛCDM, suggesting the apparent shifts may be due to statistical fluctuations.
AI.motivation: Recent DESI BAO measurements have shown a mild preference for dynamical dark energy over the standard ΛCDM model. This paper aims to investigate whether this apparent deviation is robust or could be driven by specific redshift ranges, statistical fluctuations, or the limited precision of current subsamples.
AI.method: The authors analyze the w0waCDM model using DESI BAO DR2, Pantheon+ SNe Ia, and Planck 2018 CMB distance prior data. They employ two complementary redshift-cut strategies, dividing the dataset into z<z_cut and z>z_cut subsamples to examine how different redshift ranges affect the inferred cosmological constraints and the apparent deviation from ΛCDM. They also use information criteria (AIC/BIC) and parameter-shift consistency tests.
AI.result: The most noticeable parameter shifts occur when BAO and SNe Ia data in the redshift range z~0.4–0.8 are included, reaching ~2σ significance. Including higher-redshift measurements progressively weakens this deviation and shifts constraints closer to ΛCDM. Information criteria show no statistically significant preference between w0waCDM and ΛCDM, with BIC consistently favoring ΛCDM. A parameter-shift test finds no significant tension between complementary redshift subsamples.
AI.conclusion: Within the adopted data framework, there is no statistically robust evidence favoring w0waCDM over ΛCDM. The apparent parameter shifts under different redshift cuts likely reflect statistical fluctuations and limited precision/datapoints in current subsamples. The redshift-dependent analysis provides a complementary diagnostic for assessing variation in cosmological constraints under different redshift selections.

title: Fractal properties of the cosmic web
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures. Paper presented at the Sixth Zeldovich meeting, an international conference in honour of Ya. B. Zeldovich, held in Pescara, Italy on July 13 -17, 2026. Submitted to Astronomy Reports
summary: The cosmic web is one of the most complex systems in nature, consisting of galaxies and clusters of galaxies connected by filaments and walls, and separated by large empty regions known as cosmic voids. The most common method for describing the web is the correlation function and its derivative, the structure function and fractal dimension function. In this paper I review the fractal properties of the cosmic web within the concordance ΛCDM framework. I describe how the fractal function is derived from the angular and spatial distributions of galaxies and discuss the relations between these approaches.

AI.tldr: This paper reviews the fractal properties of the cosmic web (galaxies, filaments, walls, and voids) within the standard ΛCDM cosmological framework, deriving the fractal dimension function from both angular and spatial galaxy distributions and relating these approaches.
AI.motivation: The cosmic web is one of nature's most complex systems, and the correlation function (along with its derivatives, the structure function and fractal dimension function) is the most common way to characterize it. A systematic review of fractal properties within the concordance cosmology is needed.
AI.method: The paper derives the fractal function from both angular and spatial distributions of galaxies and discusses the relationships between these two approaches within the ΛCDM framework.
AI.result: The paper provides a review of fractal properties of the cosmic web, describing how the fractal dimension function is obtained from galaxy distributions and the connection between angular and spatial derivations.
AI.conclusion: The fractal approach, built on the correlation function, provides a robust descriptor of cosmic web structure, with angular and spatial methods being related but distinct ways of quantifying the same underlying fractal geometry of the large-scale structure.

title: Non-Thermal Pressure due to Gas Motions in the Intracluster Medium: Confronting XRISM/Resolve with TNG-Cluster Simulations
comment: 16 pages, 12 Figures. Submitted to PASJ. Revised after referee's report. Comments are welcome
summary: Intracluster medium (ICM) gas motions probe cluster assembly, feedback, and non-thermal pressure support, but recent XRISM observations reveal velocity dispersions and non-thermal pressure fractions systematically lower than simulations predict, with extreme systems such as Abell 2029 falling below nearly all simulated clusters. Using the TNG-Cluster simulations, we show that the non-thermal pressure fraction depends sensitively on cool-core state and formation history, and provide a two-scale fitting function capturing both the inner cool-core suppression and outer rise of the radial profile. By forward-modeling mock XRISM observations and comparing them with both projected and intrinsic three-dimensional quantities, we find that azimuthal variations and projection effects contribute to the deficit in the observed velocity dispersion and non-thermal pressure fraction. This bias increases with radius and partially offsets the intrinsic outward rise in the true three-dimensional non-thermal pressure fraction. However, these effects cannot explain the extremely low values of the non-thermal pressure fraction observed in Abell 2029, which fall below approximately the 0th - 6th percentiles of the simulated cool-core cluster distribution at every measured radius under both the turbulence-only and turbulence-plus-bulk definitions. The remaining tension points to rare dynamical conditions or missing physics affecting the amplitude of gas motions in current ICM models.

AI.tldr: This paper uses TNG-Cluster simulations to reconcile XRISM observations of ICM gas motions showing systematically lower velocity dispersions and non-thermal pressure fractions than simulations predict. The authors find that cool-core state, formation history, azimuthal variations, and projection effects partially explain the discrepancy, but the extreme case of Abell 2029 remains unexplained, pointing to rare dynamical conditions or missing physics in current ICM models.
AI.motivation: Recent XRISM observations reveal ICM velocity dispersions and non-thermal pressure fractions systematically lower than simulation predictions, with extreme systems like Abell 2029 falling below nearly all simulated clusters. This tension challenges our understanding of cluster assembly, feedback, and non-thermal pressure support.
AI.method: The authors use TNG-Cluster simulations to: (1) show the non-thermal pressure fraction depends sensitively on cool-core state and formation history, (2) provide a two-scale fitting function capturing inner cool-core suppression and outer rise, and (3) forward-model mock XRISM observations to compare projected vs intrinsic three-dimensional quantities including the effects of azimuthal variations and projection along the line of sight.
AI.result: Azimuthal variations and projection effects contribute to the deficit in observed velocity dispersion and non-thermal pressure fraction, with this bias increasing with radius and partially offsetting the intrinsic outward rise. However, these effects cannot explain the extremely low values in Abell 2029, which fall below approximately the 0th-6th percentiles of the simulated cool-core cluster distribution at every measured radius under both turbulence-only and turbulence-plus-bulk definitions.
AI.conclusion: The remaining tension between XRISM observations and simulations points to either rare dynamical conditions or missing physics affecting the amplitude of gas motions in current ICM models, suggesting current simulations may overpredict non-thermal pressure support in galaxy clusters.

title: The most extreme high-z radio quasars in the eRASS:1 X-ray survey
comment: Accepted for pubblication on MNRAS 2026 August 04, Submitted 2026 May 25
summary: We present the selection and identification of high-z radio quasars from a combination of X-ray (eROSITA All-Sky Survey), optical/NIR (DECam Local Volume Exploration), and radio (Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey) surveys. After building a sample of 68 new high-z quasar candidates, we performed follow-up spectroscopic observations on 46 sources, confirming 39 to have redshifts z>3.5. For the subset of radio quasars at z>4, the 14 new sources identified here represent an increase of $\sim$65% in the known population of objects above the same flux limits in the same area. Using X-ray-to-optical relative intensity, we identified blazars in our sample, which we then used to compare the total number of z>4, X-ray selected blazars to the predictions of a fractional IC/CMB model previously proposed in the literature. Overall we find a relatively good agreement, even considering the potential biases in the redshift distribution from the incompleteness of the spectroscopic follow-up and the blazar classification criteria. The sources presented in this work represent a sample well suited for investigating the evolution of the most extreme systems in the early Universe, including their relativistic jets and accretion properties

AI.tldr: The paper presents the selection and spectroscopic confirmation of 39 new high-redshift radio quasars (z>3.5) identified by combining X-ray (eROSITA), optical/NIR (DECam), and radio (ASKAP) surveys. The 14 new z>4 radio quasars increase the known population above the same flux limits by ~65%. Blazars identified via X-ray-to-optical relative intensity are compared to IC/CMB model predictions, finding good agreement. These sources are well-suited for studying jet and accretion physics in the early Universe.
AI.motivation: To identify new high-redshift radio quasars by leveraging multi-wavelength survey data (X-ray, optical/NIR, radio), thereby expanding the known population of z>4 radio quasars and testing theoretical predictions about blazar populations in the early Universe.
AI.method: Cross-matching data from eROSITA All-Sky Survey (X-ray), DECam Local Volume Exploration (optical/NIR), and Rapid ASKAP Continuum Survey (radio) to build a sample of 68 high-z quasar candidates, followed by spectroscopic follow-up of 46 sources. Blazars are identified using X-ray-to-optical relative intensity and compared to predictions of a fractional IC/CMB model.
AI.result: 39 of 46 spectroscopically followed sources were confirmed at z>3.5. The 14 new radio quasars at z>4 represent a ~65% increase in the known population at the same flux limits and sky area. The observed number of X-ray selected z>4 blazars shows good agreement with fractional IC/CMB model predictions, accounting for observational biases.
AI.conclusion: Multi-wavelength selection from combined X-ray, optical/NIR, and radio surveys is an effective strategy for discovering high-z radio quasars. The new sample provides a valuable resource for studying the most extreme systems in the early Universe, including relativistic jets and accretion properties, and supports the fractional IC/CMB model for high-redshift blazar evolution.

title: Is Dark Matter Really Matter?
comment: 7+6 pages, 6 figures
summary: In the standard model of cosmology, it is assumed that dark matter is pressureless with equation of state $w=0$ and dark energy has $w=-1$. We test these assumptions jointly using DESI DR2 distance measurements, including the recent Lyman-$α$ full-shape Alcock-Paczynski (AP) information, DES supernovae, and two complementary CMB treatment. When constant $w_{dm}$ and $w_{de}$ are varied together, we find $w_{dm}=0.000968^{+0.000501}_{-0.000496}$ and $w_{de}=-0.9380^{+0.0259}_{-0.0262}$ (68%). With an alternative CMB treatment that marginalizes over the lensing spectrum, the corresponding constraints are $w_{dm}=0.000870^{+0.000408}_{-0.000410}$ and $w_{de}=-0.9353^{+0.0258}_{-0.0254}$. Both standard $Λ$CDM values are disfavored at approximately $2σ$ in the joint extension. Neither parameter departs significantly from its standard value when only that parameter is varied. This behavior arises because late-time distances favor $w_{de}>-1$, while maintaining the early-Universe physical matter density requires a compensating positive $w_{dm}$, which changes the mapping to the matter density today. Allowing dynamical dark energy clarify further on complexity of the situation: phantom crossing for dark energy makes $w_{dm}=0$ consistent with the data, whereas a positive $w_{dm}$ preference persists when crossing is forbidden. Interestingly, the Pad'e-$w$ parameterization that provides a flexible description of a class of quintessence models (with no phantom crossing), along with $w_{dm}$ free, is even mildly favored over the phantom-crossing $w_0w_a$ model according to both the best-fit $χ^2$ and the DIC under both CMB treatments. One can conclude that the apparent preference for phantom crossing may instead reflect deviations in the dark-matter sector rather than dark-energy dynamics alone. [abridged]

AI.tldr: This paper jointly tests the standard cosmological assumptions that dark matter is pressureless (w_dm=0) and dark energy has w_de=-1 using DESI DR2 distance measurements, Lyman-α full-shape AP information, DES supernovae, and two CMB treatments. When both parameters are varied together, the data find w_dm slightly positive (~0.0009) and w_de slightly above -1 (~-0.94), disfavoring standard ΛCDM values at ~2σ. The results suggest that apparent phantom-crossing preferences in dark energy may instead reflect deviations in the dark matter sector.
AI.motivation: The standard cosmological model assumes dark matter has equation of state w=0 and dark energy has w=-1. The authors aim to jointly test both of these assumptions using the latest DESI DR2 data (including Lyman-α AP information) and complementary cosmological probes, to see whether deviations in the dark matter sector could be masquerading as dark energy dynamics.
AI.method: The authors perform joint cosmological parameter estimation using DESI DR2 distance measurements (including recent Lyman-α full-shape Alcock-Paczynski information), DES supernovae, and two complementary CMB treatments. They vary constant w_dm and w_de together, and also consider dynamical dark energy parameterizations (w0wa and Padé-w) both with and without phantom crossing, allowing w_dm to be free. Model comparison uses best-fit χ² and the Deviance Information Criterion (DIC).
AI.result: With both w_dm and w_de varied, w_dm=0.000968±0.0005 and w_de=-0.938±0.026 (68%). An alternative CMB treatment marginalizing over lensing gives w_dm=0.000870±0.0004 and w_de=-0.935±0.026. Standard ΛCDM values are disfavored at ~2σ in the joint extension, though neither departs significantly when only one parameter is varied. This is explained by late-time distances favoring w_de>-1 while maintaining the early-Universe physical matter density requires a compensating positive w_dm. Phantom crossing makes w_dm=0 consistent with data, whereas a positive w_dm preference persists without crossing. The Padé-w quintessence parameterization (no crossing) with free w_dm is mildly favored over the phantom-crossing w0wa model in both χ² and DIC.
AI.conclusion: The apparent preference for phantom crossing in dark energy may instead reflect deviations in the dark-matter sector rather than dark-energy dynamics alone. A positive w_dm (slightly non-pressureless dark matter) with a quintessence-like dark energy (no phantom crossing) can fit the data comparably or better than phantom-crossing models, suggesting the standard ΛCDM assumptions on both components may require revision.

title: The Most Dangerous Seed: Nonlinear Optimal Perturbations in Rayleigh-Taylor Instability
comment: 15 pages, 7 figures, submitted to ApJ
summary: Long-term instabilities in astrophysical fluids are inherently nonlinear, where even small-amplitude perturbations can trigger dramatic instability. However, owing to the complex interactions among non-normal modes, the perturbation structures responsible for the greatest growth remain poorly understood. In this paper, we employ the nonlinear optimization method known as the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) to identify the most dangerous initial velocity perturbation, i.e., the perturbation that maximizes the kinetic energy growth in the two-dimensional compressible Rayleigh-Taylor instability in astrophysical hydrodynamics. Compared with random perturbations, the optimal perturbation forms a coherent wave-packet structure localized around the density interface. We investigate its dependence on spatial resolution and optimization time horizon through two sets of numerical experiments. For a fixed optimization time, increasing the spatial resolution produces a more sharply localized wave packet, whereas for a fixed spatial resolution, increasing the optimization time causes the wave packet to become progressively more dispersed. Furthermore, we analyze the optimal perturbations in Fourier space using the fast Fourier transform (FFT), which provides a clearer characterization of the spectral distribution. Higher-resolution simulations concentrate most of the perturbation energy into only a few dominant modes, while longer optimization times distribute the energy over a broader range of modes. These results indicate that short optimization time horizons involve relatively weak modal interactions and remain closer to the linear regime, whereas longer optimization times enhance nonlinear modal interactions, broaden the spectral distribution, and reduce the predictive capability of linear stability theory.

AI.tldr: This paper uses the conditional nonlinear optimal perturbation (CNOP) method to identify the most dangerous initial velocity perturbation that maximizes kinetic energy growth in two-dimensional compressible Rayleigh-Taylor instability, revealing that optimal perturbations form coherent wave packets localized around the density interface, with characteristics dependent on spatial resolution and optimization time horizon.
AI.motivation: The perturbation structures responsible for the greatest growth in nonlinear astrophysical fluid instabilities, such as Rayleigh-Taylor instability, remain poorly understood due to complex interactions among non-normal modes.
AI.method: The authors employ the nonlinear optimization method CNOP to find the initial velocity perturbation maximizing kinetic energy growth in 2D compressible Rayleigh-Taylor instability. They conduct two sets of numerical experiments varying spatial resolution and optimization time horizon, and analyze the optimal perturbations in Fourier space using fast Fourier transform (FFT).
AI.result: Optimal perturbations form coherent wave packets localized around the density interface, unlike random perturbations. Higher spatial resolution produces sharper localization while longer optimization times disperse the wave packet. In Fourier space, higher-resolution simulations concentrate energy into few dominant modes, while longer optimization times broaden the spectral distribution.
AI.conclusion: Short optimization time horizons remain closer to the linear regime with relatively weak modal interactions, whereas longer optimization times enhance nonlinear modal interactions, broaden the spectral distribution, and reduce the predictive capability of linear stability theory.

title: Characterising the epoch of reionisation using the cross-correlation of the kSZ effect and CMB lensing
summary: We investigate the cross-correlation of the kinematic Sunyaev-Zeldovich (kSZ) effect with lensing of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) as a probe of the epoch of reionisation. During reionisation, bubbles of ionised electrons form around overdensities, generating temperature perturbations in the CMB via the kSZ effect, which correlate with the projected matter density field probed by CMB lensing. We demonstrate using AMBER simulations that this effect can be probed via cross-correlating the squared kSZ field with the CMB lensing potential, and that the signal is sensitive to the duration and midpoint of reionisation. We forecast that for a Simons Observatory-like experiment with 5$μ$K-arcmin white noise, covering 40% of the sky, the signal could be marginally detected at $S/N$ = 2 to 3. Meanwhile, a futuristic experiment like CMB-HD could provide a measurement of $S/N \sim 50$, yielding informative constraints on reionisation scenarios. We investigate potential challenges in measuring the signal and explore mitigation for each: contamination from extragalactic foregrounds at low redshift, contamination of the kSZ-squared estimator by lensing, and other estimator biases.

AI.tldr: This paper proposes cross-correlating the squared kinematic Sunyaev-Zeldovich (kSZ) field with CMB lensing as a new probe of the epoch of reionisation. Using AMBER simulations, they show the signal is sensitive to reionisation duration and midpoint, forecast marginal detection (S/N=2-3) for Simons Observatory-like experiments and strong constraints (S/N~50) for futuristic CMB-HD-class experiments, and explore mitigation strategies for foreground contamination, lensing contamination of the kSZ-squared estimator, and other biases.
AI.motivation: The epoch of reionisation is a poorly constrained period of cosmic history. The authors aim to develop a new observable—the cross-correlation between the kSZ effect and CMB lensing—that can provide constraints on reionisation duration and midpoint, complementing existing probes.
AI.method: The authors use AMBER simulations to demonstrate that the kSZ field squared, when cross-correlated with the CMB lensing potential, carries information about the reionisation process. They forecast detectability for Simons Observatory-like and CMB-HD-like experimental configurations and analyze systematic challenges including extragalactic foreground contamination, lensing contamination of the kSZ-squared estimator, and other estimator biases, proposing mitigation strategies for each.
AI.result: The signal is sensitive to reionisation duration and midpoint. A Simons Observatory-like experiment (5μK-arcmin white noise, 40% sky) could marginally detect the signal at S/N=2-3, while a futuristic CMB-HD experiment could achieve S/N~50, providing informative reionisation constraints.
AI.conclusion: The kSZ-lensing cross-correlation is a viable and promising new probe of the epoch of reionisation. While current and near-term experiments may only marginally detect the signal, futuristic high-sensitivity, high-resolution CMB experiments could yield powerful constraints on reionisation scenarios once systematic challenges are properly mitigated.

title: Predicting the Kinematics of the Cold Circumgalactic Medium from its Morphology using Convolutional Neural Networks
comment: 18 pages, 8 figures
summary: We present a novel approach to predicting plane-of-sky velocities of cold gas clouds in the circumgalactic medium (CGM) of galaxies. The method uses a convolutional neural network (CNN) trained on simulated emission maps derived from the TNG50 cosmological simulation, with forward modeled noise properties consistent with upcoming observational facilities. Using 182 Milky Way/Andromeda analog galaxies, we generate emission maps in H$α$ using $\texttt{Cloudy}$ models, as well as line-of-sight averaged 2D velocity maps. Using a UNet architecture, we train the CNN to take emission maps as input and return plane-of-sky velocity maps as output, which cannot be observationally constrained using traditional methods. Qualitatively, the model is generally able to infer the true overall flow direction. We quantify the effects of Gaussian noise on the network's training and predictive power. At depths expected to be probed by forthcoming telescopes such as MOTHRA, the network has a typical RMS error for the plane-of-sky velocity direction of $0.3-0.5 v_{vir}$. This implies that 2D emission maps of sufficient depths will be able to estimate two additional phase space dimensions of cold CGM gas, enabling targeted followup and a better understanding of overall CGM flows.

AI.tldr: A CNN (UNet) trained on TNG50 simulation data with Cloudy-generated Hα emission maps can predict plane-of-sky velocities of cold CGM gas clouds, achieving typical RMS errors of 0.3–0.5 v_vir at depths accessible by upcoming telescopes like MOTHRA, thereby enabling two additional phase-space dimensions to be inferred from 2D emission maps.
AI.motivation: The plane-of-sky velocities of cold gas clouds in the circumgalactic medium cannot be measured with traditional observational methods, limiting our understanding of CGM flows and the missing phase-space information.
AI.method: The authors train a convolutional neural network with a UNet architecture on 182 Milky Way/Andromeda analog galaxies from the TNG50 cosmological simulation. Emission maps in Hα are generated using Cloudy models, paired with line-of-sight averaged 2D velocity maps. The CNN takes emission maps as input and outputs plane-of-sky velocity maps; Gaussian noise is forward-modeled to match upcoming observational facilities, and its effect on training and prediction is quantified.
AI.result: The model can infer the overall flow direction of cold CGM gas. At depths expected for telescopes such as MOTHRA, the network achieves a typical RMS error of 0.3–0.5 v_vir for plane-of-sky velocity direction.
AI.conclusion: Deep enough 2D emission maps can estimate two additional phase-space dimensions of cold CGM gas, enabling targeted follow-up observations and an improved understanding of overall CGM flows.

title: Coupled quintessence from an axion dark sector
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, 2 tables
summary: Recent observational data arising from the DESI collaboration has hinted at a possible departure from the standard $Λ$CDM cosmological model, preferring instead the presence of a dynamical dark energy component. Specifically, the associated equation of state of the dark energy features a crossing into the so-called phantom regime, which is challenging to accommodate in canonical single scalar-field scenarios. However, this behavior can be effectively described by an interacting dark sector, where the specific dark energy equation of state remains above the phantom divide whilst the dark matter component deviates from the standard cold dark matter evolution. In this work, we explore this possibility in the context of an axion dark sector, where both the dark energy and dark matter are represented by two interacting axion-like fields. We show that given the required mass hierarchy for these fields to play such roles, their dynamics can be effectively placed in the coupled quintessence framework, where their motion follows from a sourced continuity equation in the fluid description. In this regime, we perform a statistical analysis of this scenario with current data, finding that a sub-Planckian dark energy axion decay constant stays well within the observational bounds without the need to fine-tune the associated field's initial conditions. We also perform a comparison with $Λ$CDM, where we find that the model provides a better fit to the data while staying competitive from a Bayesian perspective.

AI.tldr: The paper explores an interacting axion dark sector model with two axion-like fields representing dark energy and dark matter to explain the DESI hint of dynamical dark energy (including phantom crossing) without violating the phantom divide in the dark energy equation of state. A statistical analysis shows the model fits current data better than ΛCDM and remains Bayesian competitive without fine-tuning.
AI.motivation: DESI observational data hints at dynamical dark energy with an equation of state crossing into the phantom regime, which is difficult to accommodate in canonical single scalar-field models. The authors aim to explain this behavior through an interacting dark sector where dark energy stays above the phantom divide while dark matter deviates from cold dark matter evolution.
AI.method: Two interacting axion-like fields represent dark energy and dark matter. Given the required mass hierarchy, the dynamics are placed in the coupled quintessence framework with a sourced continuity equation in the fluid description. A statistical analysis of the scenario is performed against current observational data.
AI.result: A sub-Planckian dark energy axion decay constant remains well within observational bounds without fine-tuning the field's initial conditions. The model provides a better fit to the data than ΛCDM while remaining competitive from a Bayesian perspective.
AI.conclusion: The interacting axion dark sector model can effectively describe the DESI phantom-crossing hint while keeping the dark energy equation of state above the phantom divide, offering a viable and statistically competitive alternative to ΛCDM.

title: Column-Density Estimation from the Equivalent Widths of Absorption Doublets
comment: 13 pages, 2 figures, 2 tables. Submitted to MNRAS
summary: Na I D absorption is widely used to estimate the dust extinction toward Galactic and extragalactic sources, but the inferred column densities are unreliable once the lines saturate. We present an analytical framework for estimating column densities from the equivalent widths ($EW$s) of absorption-line doublets. The method requires only that the two doublet members be measured separately -- the velocity structure need not be resolved -- so a resolving power $λ/Δλ\gtrsim10^{3}$ suffices for Na I D, two orders of magnitude below velocity-resolved methods. For the Gaussian curve of growth, the classical inversion reduces to a universal saturation correction depending only on the doublet ratio, $R=EW_2/EW_1$: at fixed $R$, the inferred column density is linear in the measured $EW$. The formulation yields the exact Gaussian inversion, $N_{\tildeκ}$, which provides the Doppler parameter; a closed-form second-order approximation; and a strict lower bound, $N_{\rm min}$, valid for an arbitrary velocity structure. We recommend reporting $N_{\rm min}$: an optimal, assumption-free lower bound, within a few per cent of $N_{\tildeκ}$ for $R\gtrsim1.4$ and at most a factor $3.5$ below it at $R=1.1$. The ratio $N_{\tildeκ}/N_{\rm 2nd}$ provides a per-object saturation diagnostic. We validate the framework against published profile-fitting Na I D column densities toward Type Ia supernovae, using only the integrated $EW$s. An explicit closed-form formula converts the two $EW$s into an extinction estimate through the observed $\log N(\mathrm{Na\,I})$--$A_V$ relation. A public implementation with full uncertainty propagation accompanies the paper.

AI.tldr: Presents an analytical framework for estimating column densities from equivalent widths of absorption-line doublets, robust to saturation, requiring only moderate resolving power. Provides exact Gaussian inversion, a closed-form approximation, a strict lower bound valid for arbitrary velocity structure, and validation against Na I D observations toward Type Ia supernovae.
AI.motivation: Na I D absorption is widely used to estimate dust extinction, but inferred column densities become unreliable once the lines saturate. Existing velocity-resolved methods require high spectral resolution, which is not always available.
AI.method: The method inverts the equivalent widths of the two doublet members separately (using their ratio R) to recover column densities without resolving velocity structure. It derives an exact Gaussian inversion N_tilde-kappa, a second-order closed-form approximation, and a strict lower bound N_min valid for arbitrary velocity structure. A saturation diagnostic uses the ratio N_tilde-kappa/N_2nd.
AI.result: The framework requires only resolving power ~10^3 (two orders of magnitude below velocity-resolved methods). N_min is within a few percent of the exact Gaussian inversion for R >= 1.4 and at most a factor 3.5 below at R=1.1. The method is validated against profile-fitting Na I D column densities toward Type Ia supernovae using only integrated EWs, and provides a closed-form extinction estimate via the log N(Na I)-A_V relation.
AI.conclusion: The framework offers an optimal, assumption-free lower bound N_min for column density estimation from doublet EWs, with a public implementation and full uncertainty propagation, making it broadly applicable for extinction studies at moderate spectral resolution.

title: Inflow-driven galaxy evolution - I. Revealing the physics of the fundamental metallicity relation
comment: 29 pages, 17 + 2 figures. Presents a unified framework for the fundamental metallicity relation, with a physical picture in Sec. 3, an analytic derivation in Sec. 4, and a comparison to previous models and observations in Sec. 5
summary: We present a unified physical framework for the fundamental metallicity relation (FMR), based on the mass-continuity equations. The FMR is not merely the anti-correlation between star formation rate (SFR) and gas metallicity ($Z_{\rm g}$) at fixed stellar mass ($M_\star$); it is a redshift-invariant surface in the $(M_\star,{\rm SFR},Z_{\rm g})$ space. We construct a minimal cosmological gas flow model, calibrated to reproduce the mass-metallicity relation, star-forming main sequence, and stellar-to-halo mass relation at $z=0-3$, and show that the FMR emerges as a prediction of the calibrated physics. Through controlled experiments that progressively simplify the model, we reveal that in a universe where both the star formation efficiency ($ε$) and mass-loading factor ($η$) are constants, the FMR reduces to a universal scaling between $Z_{\rm g}$ and $M_\star/$SFR, whose shape traces the transition from inflow-driven regime to equilibrium. The specific parameterisation of the observed FMR is not a fundamental symmetry but a contingent consequence of how $ε$ and $η$ depend on stellar mass and redshift. We show that the gaseous FMR (gFMR), defined in the $(M_\star,M_{\rm g},Z_{\rm g})$ space, is more fundamental than the standard FMR: in the inflow-driven limit, $Z_{\rm g}$ is proportional to $M_\star/M_{\rm g}$, and the approach to equilibrium is governed by $M_\star/M_{\rm g}$ and $η$ alone. We derive an analytic solution for an idealised version of the model that provides closed-form expressions relating $Z_{\rm g}$, $M_{\rm g}/M_\star$, and $η$, and show this framework accurately reproduces the cosmological gas flow model. By establishing the physical origin of the FMR and its connection to the more fundamental gFMR, we provide the theoretical foundation to turn metallicity scaling relations into precision probes of the baryon cycle over cosmic history.

AI.tldr: The paper presents a unified physical framework for the fundamental metallicity relation (FMR) based on mass-continuity equations, showing that the FMR emerges as a prediction of a calibrated cosmological gas flow model rather than being a fundamental symmetry. The authors reveal that while the FMR is a redshift-invariant surface in (M*, SFR, Zg) space, it is a contingent consequence of how star formation efficiency (ε) and mass-loading factor (η) depend on stellar mass and redshift. They introduce the gaseous FMR (gFMR) in (M*, Mg, Zg) space as more fundamental, derive an analytic solution for an idealized model, and provide closed-form relations connecting Zg, Mg/M*, and η.
AI.motivation: To establish the physical origin of the fundamental metallicity relation and provide a theoretical foundation for using metallicity scaling relations as precision probes of the baryon cycle over cosmic history, rather than treating the FMR as an empirical or coincidental relation.
AI.method: The authors construct a minimal cosmological gas flow model based on mass-continuity equations, calibrated to reproduce the mass-metallicity relation, star-forming main sequence, and stellar-to-halo mass relation at z=0-3. They perform controlled experiments that progressively simplify the model, compare constant versus variable ε and η, and derive an analytic solution for an idealized version of the model providing closed-form expressions relating Zg, Mg/M*, and η.
AI.result: The FMR emerges as a prediction of the calibrated gas flow physics, not as a fundamental symmetry. When ε and η are constants, the FMR reduces to a universal scaling between Zg and M*/SFR whose shape traces the inflow-driven-to-equilibrium transition. The gaseous FMR (gFMR) in (M*, Mg, Zg) space is shown to be more fundamental, with Zg proportional to M*/Mg in the inflow-driven limit. The analytic solution accurately reproduces the cosmological gas flow model.
AI.conclusion: The FMR's specific parameterization is a contingent consequence of how ε and η depend on stellar mass and redshift. The gFMR is more fundamental than the standard FMR, and this framework provides the theoretical basis to turn metallicity scaling relations into precision probes of the baryon cycle across cosmic history.

title: Implications of Broad [O III] 4364 and UV Line Emission in Two Little Red Dots at z ~ 7 - 8
comment: Submitted to ApJ; 24 pages, 14 figures. Comments welcome
summary: We present deep, NIRSpec G140M and G395M spectroscopy of Little Red Dots (LRDs) at z = 6.68 and z = 8.35. Both LRDs show broad Balmer and [O III] $λ$4364 emission. The broad [O III] $λ$4364 lines have FWHM ~1000 km/s, about 1/3 that of the H$β$ lines. Assuming gas temperatures T ~ 15,000 - 25,000 K, the [O III] $λ$4364/[O III] $λ$5008 ratios of the broad lines yield high gas densities, log n/cm^-3 = 6.3 to 7.9, 3-10$\times$ higher than those in broad-line regions of low-redshift quasars. If the broad-lines trace virial motions, it is evidence for metal-enhanced gas clouds, ~1-10~pc from the LRD engine. Both LRDs show narrow [C III] $λ$1907 + C III] $λ$1909, and O III] $λλ$1661,1666. The C III] ratios yield narrow-line gas densities, log n/cm^-3 = 4.2-5.2, similar to those in other star-forming galaxies. The line equivalent widths, EW(O III]), EW(C III]), are at, or exceed, limits expected for stellar populations, likely requiring an additional ionizing source. The LRDs also have [O III] $λ$4364/H$γ$ ratios that favor ionization from an accretion disk, possibly combined with stars. Both LRDs show nitrogen enhancement based on detections of N III] $λ$1746 or N IV] $λ$1486, which may imply rapid, recent star-formation. These results favor a scenario where the LRD gas envelopes are highly stratified, having high-density clouds with a non-unity covering factors and a complex geometry, such that ionizing radiation from the LRD accretion disk, combined with that from star-forming regions, produce the nebular emission features.

AI.tldr: Deep NIRSpec G140M and G395M spectroscopy of two Little Red Dots (LRDs) at z = 6.68 and z = 8.35 reveals broad Balmer and [O III] λ4364 lines with high gas densities (log n = 6.3-7.9 cm⁻³) indicating a highly stratified gas envelope, narrow C III] and O III] lines from lower-density gas (log n = 4.2-5.2 cm⁻³), nitrogen enhancement, and nebular emission likely powered by a combination of an accretion disk and star-forming regions.
AI.motivation: To characterize the physical conditions of Little Red Dots at high redshift through deep spectroscopy, determining gas densities, ionization sources, and the geometry/structure of their emission-line regions to understand their nature.
AI.method: Deep NIRSpec G140M and G395M spectroscopy of two LRDs at z = 6.68 and z = 8.35. Measurements of broad and narrow emission lines (Balmer, [O III] λ4364, [O III] λ5008, C III], O III], N III], N IV]) to derive gas densities via line ratios, assuming gas temperatures T ~ 15,000-25,000 K, and comparing line equivalent widths and ionization ratios to stellar and accretion disk models.
AI.result: Broad lines show high densities (log n = 6.3-7.9 cm⁻³), 3-10× higher than low-z quasar broad-line regions, with virial motions implying metal-enriched clouds ~1-10 pc from the LRD engine. Narrow lines indicate lower densities (log n = 4.2-5.2 cm⁻³). Line EWs exceed stellar limits, requiring an additional ionizing source. [O III] λ4364/Hγ ratios favor accretion-disk ionization possibly combined with stars. Both LRDs show nitrogen enhancement.
AI.conclusion: The LRD gas envelopes are highly stratified with high-density clouds of non-unity covering factors and complex geometry, where ionizing radiation from the accretion disk combined with star-forming regions produces the observed nebular emission.

title: Resolving dense photo-dissociation regions: the structure of photochemical fronts in three-dimensional gas distributions
comment: Re-submitted to A&A following first referee report. Comments welcome
summary: For decades, the Orion Bar has been the prototypical photo-dissociation region. Viewed nearly edge-on, it offers a unique window into the stratified chemical structure of the atomic-to-molecular transition of the interstellar medium. Understanding its photochemistry is essential to interpreting key observations originating from dense photo-dissociation regions. ALMA and JWST observations reveal that H2 photo-dissociation front overlaps with the C+ recombination front and exhibits a complex spatial morphology. Despite considerable theoretical effort, existing modeling approaches based on simplified geometrical assumptions have difficulties reproducing the spatial emission structure. Our aim is to investigate the response of photochemistry in realistic three-dimensional density distributions, using the Orion Bar as a representative application. We present the first fully three-dimensional high-resolution model of an Orion Bar analogue that resolves the relevant photochemical fronts using the upgraded steady-state 3D-PDR photo-dissociation region code, which allows for the treatment of plane-irradiatation and for the solution of the non-LTE H2 rovibrational levels. We find that the H2 dissociation front is characterized by a complex surface that overlaps with the C+ recombination front. Our 3D model can reproduce the complex morphology of H2 emission seen in observations, in particular the arc- and filament-like features, and provides a physical explanation of its chemistry. The overlapping H2 dissociation and C+ recombination fronts and the spatial emission morphology can be explained due to the three-dimensional gas distribution, resulting in shadowing and shielding by dense substructures. Our results mark a turning point for astrochemistry, where three-dimensional steady-state models can deliver fundamentally new insights into the chemistry of the interstellar medium.

AI.tldr: This paper presents the first fully three-dimensional, high-resolution model of an Orion Bar analogue using the upgraded steady-state 3D-PDR code, which reproduces the complex spatial morphology of H2 emission (arc- and filament-like features) observed by ALMA and JWST, showing that the overlap of H2 dissociation and C+ recombination fronts is explained by shadowing and shielding from dense 3D gas substructures.
AI.motivation: The Orion Bar is the prototypical photo-dissociation region, yet existing 2D/simplified geometry models cannot reproduce the complex spatial emission structure revealed by ALMA and JWST, where the H2 dissociation front overlaps with the C+ recombination front. There is a need to investigate photochemistry in realistic 3D density distributions.
AI.method: The authors used the upgraded steady-state 3D-PDR photo-dissociation region code, which supports plane-irradiation treatment and solves the non-LTE H2 rovibrational levels, to build a fully three-dimensional high-resolution model of an Orion Bar analogue that resolves the relevant photochemical fronts.
AI.result: The 3D model reproduces the complex H2 emission morphology observed, including arc- and filament-like features. It shows that the H2 dissociation front is a complex surface overlapping with the C+ recombination front, and explains the spatial emission morphology through shadowing and shielding by dense 3D substructures.
AI.conclusion: The results mark a turning point for astrochemistry, demonstrating that three-dimensional steady-state models can deliver fundamentally new insights into interstellar medium chemistry, with the overlapping fronts and complex morphology explained by 3D gas distribution effects.

title: Chemo-dynamical stratification of the Galactic disc using \emph{Gaia}-ESO open clusters
comment: 15 pages, 7 main Figures and two appendix figures
summary: Understanding how the Milky Way disc assembled and evolved requires tracing the coupled evolution of stellar chemistry and orbital structure over time. Open clusters, as coeval stellar populations with well-constrained ages, distances, and chemical properties, provide powerful benchmarks for this purpose. We aim to characterise the age-dependent chemo-dynamical structure of the Galactic disc and to investigate how open clusters populate dynamical phase space as a function of age. We analysed a sample of Galactic open clusters using homogeneous chemical abundances from the Gaia-ESO Survey together with Gaia DR3 phase-space information. Combining cluster ages with orbital parameters and actions, we examined how clusters populate dynamical phase space over the last ~4 Gyr. We find that clusters with similar chemical properties occupy coherent regions of action space, while their orbital structure shows a clear dependence on age. Radial excursions and orbital eccentricities broaden systematically toward older ages, indicating increasingly diverse orbital configurations in the older cluster population. The dispersion in the [Fe/H]-Rg relation also increases with age, consistent with a combination of secular redistribution, survival bias, and dynamically distinct outer-disc populations. In addition, older clusters reach larger vertical amplitudes and vertical actions, revealing a coupled but anisotropic evolution between in-plane and vertical orbital structure. Open clusters provide precise, age-resolved tracers of the chemo-dynamical structure of the Galactic disc. Our results reveal systematic age-dependent variations in the orbital and chemical properties of the cluster population, consistent with the combined effects of secular evolution, orbital redistribution, and environmentally dependent cluster survival over the last few Gyr.

AI.tldr: This study uses Gaia-ESO Survey chemical abundances and Gaia DR3 phase-space data to analyze Galactic open clusters, revealing that cluster orbital structure (radial excursions, eccentricities, vertical amplitudes) broadens systematically with age, while chemical-dynamical coherence in action space is maintained among chemically similar clusters.
AI.motivation: Understanding how the Milky Way disc assembled requires tracing the coupled evolution of stellar chemistry and orbital structure over time. Open clusters serve as coeval stellar populations with well-constrained ages, distances, and chemical properties, making them powerful benchmarks for probing disc assembly and evolution.
AI.method: The authors combined homogeneous chemical abundances from the Gaia-ESO Survey with Gaia DR3 phase-space information for a sample of Galactic open clusters. They computed orbital parameters and actions, combining these with cluster ages to examine how clusters populate dynamical phase space over the last ~4 Gyr.
AI.result: Clusters with similar chemical properties occupy coherent regions of action space. Radial excursions and orbital eccentricities broaden toward older ages, indicating increasingly diverse orbital configurations. The dispersion in the [Fe/H]-Rg relation increases with age, and older clusters reach larger vertical amplitudes and vertical actions, revealing coupled but anisotropic evolution between in-plane and vertical orbital structure.
AI.conclusion: Open clusters provide precise, age-resolved tracers of the chemo-dynamical structure of the Galactic disc. The systematic age-dependent variations in orbital and chemical properties are consistent with secular evolution, orbital redistribution, and environmentally dependent cluster survival over the last few Gyr.

title: Phosphorous in the moderately metal-poor bulge globular clusters NGC 6539 and NGC 6569
comment: 28 pages, 8 figures
summary:
The distinct stellar populations of the Galactic bulge can be disentangled through detailed analysis of their chemical abundances and kinematical properties. Recent studies have suggested that globular clusters located in the Galactic bulge with metallicities around $\rm [Fe/H] \approx -0.7$, may represent some of the oldest systems in the Milky Way, potentially tracing the early spheroidal bulge. The coincidence of a metallicity peak at $\rm [Fe/H] \approx -0.7$ in both field stars and globular clusters, together with the presence of phosphorus-rich (P-rich) stars, may provide important clues to the nature of the first generations of stars formed in the Galaxy.
  In this work, we investigate the odd-Z elements Na, Al and particularly P in the bulge globular clusters NGC~6539 ($\rm[Fe/H] \sim -0.75$) and NGC~6569 ($\rm [Fe/H] \sim -0.85$) using APOGEE spectra. We also examine the clusters Tonantzintla-1 and NGC~6316, which exhibit evidence of phosphorus enhancement. Our analysis confirms that NGC~6539 is a cluster of interest, with one clearly P-rich star, whereas NGC~6569 shows a lower level of P-enhancement. This again suggests that there might have been an early bulge building block with the metallicity of $\rm[Fe/H] \sim-0.75$, of which NGC~6539 would be part of.
  The observed abundance patterns indicate that the production of Na and Al is consistent with nucleosynthesis in massive stars. However, the origin of the phosphorus enrichment remains uncertain, suggesting that additional nucleosynthetic channels may be required to explain the observed abundances. These findings provide new constraints on the chemical evolution of the Galactic bulge and the nature of its earliest stellar populations.

AI.tldr: This study investigates odd-Z elements (Na, Al, P) in Galactic bulge globular clusters NGC 6539 and NGC 6569 using APOGEE spectra, confirming NGC 6539 hosts a clearly P-rich star while NGC 6569 shows lower P-enhancement. The results suggest these clusters may trace an early bulge building block at [Fe/H] ~ -0.75, with Na and Al production consistent with massive star nucleosynthesis but P enrichment requiring additional nucleosynthetic channels.
AI.motivation: To disentangle the distinct stellar populations of the Galactic bulge and understand the nature of its earliest stellar generations, particularly by studying phosphorus-rich stars and globular clusters at [Fe/H] ≈ -0.7, which may represent the oldest systems in the Milky Way tracing the early spheroidal bulge.
AI.method: Analysis of APOGEE spectra for the bulge globular clusters NGC 6539 ([Fe/H] ~ -0.75) and NGC 6569 ([Fe/H] ~ -0.85), measuring the odd-Z elements Na, Al, and particularly P. Additional examination of Tonantzintla-1 and NGC 6316, which show evidence of phosphorus enhancement.
AI.result: NGC 6539 is confirmed as a cluster of interest with one clearly P-rich star, while NGC 6569 shows a lower level of P-enhancement. Observed Na and Al abundances are consistent with nucleosynthesis in massive stars, but the origin of P enrichment remains uncertain, requiring additional nucleosynthetic channels.
AI.conclusion: The findings support the possibility of an early bulge building block at [Fe/H] ~ -0.75, of which NGC 6539 may be a part. They provide new constraints on the chemical evolution of the Galactic bulge and the nature of its earliest stellar populations, though the nucleosynthetic origin of phosphorus enrichment requires further investigation.

title: Effect of non-spherical projectiles on the structure of porous dust aggregates formed by coagulation
comment: 14 pages and 9 figures
summary: Cosmic dust is ubiquitous in the universe, yet the structure and geometry of individual grains remain poorly understood. The existence of non-spherical, fluffy, and even fractal grain structures is predicted by numerical simulation and supported by observations of linear polarization of starlight. However, it has proven challenging to go beyond a qualitative investigation of such crucial grain characteristics. We present soft-sphere discrete element simulations of dust coagulation with sequential collisions using non-spherical projectiles of various sizes. We study the internal structure and geometry of the resulting aggregates under three growth conditions: a constant final aggregate size, a constant number of projectiles, and a constant projectile size. In most cases we allow for projectile internal restructuring, but we also test the effect of enforcing a constant projectile structure after impact. We find that aggregates' porosity and fractal dimension depend both on the size and number of projectiles, and that their asymmetry and stretch parameters depend more on the number of projectiles than on projectile size. Overall, the grain porosity increases with both the number of projectiles and the size of the individual projectiles. Comparison with constraints from interstellar polarization indicates that none of our sufficiently large aggregates have structures capable of reproducing the observed polarization of starlight in the interstellar medium. We conclude that cosmic dust undergoes additional processing after coagulation to acquire structures consistent with observations.

AI.tldr: The paper uses soft-sphere discrete element simulations of dust coagulation with non-spherical projectiles to study the internal structure and geometry of cosmic dust aggregates. It finds that porosity and fractal dimension depend on projectile size and number, while asymmetry depends more on projectile count. None of the simulated aggregates can reproduce interstellar polarization observations, suggesting additional dust processing occurs after coagulation.
AI.motivation: Cosmic dust grains are poorly understood in terms of their structure and geometry. While numerical simulations and observations predict non-spherical, fluffy, fractal grain structures, it has been challenging to go beyond qualitative investigation of these crucial grain characteristics.
AI.method: Soft-sphere discrete element simulations of dust coagulation with sequential collisions using non-spherical projectiles of various sizes. Three growth conditions were studied: constant final aggregate size, constant number of projectiles, and constant projectile size. Most cases allowed projectile internal restructuring, with a test case enforcing constant projectile structure after impact.
AI.result: Aggregates' porosity and fractal dimension depend on both the size and number of projectiles, while asymmetry and stretch parameters depend more on the number of projectiles than on projectile size. Grain porosity increases with both the number of projectiles and their individual size. Crucially, none of the sufficiently large aggregates can reproduce the observed polarization of starlight in the interstellar medium.
AI.conclusion: Cosmic dust must undergo additional processing after coagulation in order to acquire structures consistent with interstellar polarization observations.

title: Cold Dark Matter and Self-Interacting Dark Matter Interpretations of Cloud-9
comment: 10 pages, 6 figures
summary: Recently, the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope discovered a gas-rich hydrogen cloud near M94 in the $21\,{\rm cm}$ band. Lacking an optical counterpart, this object, dubbed Cloud-9, has been identified as a compelling Reionization Limited \textsc{Hi} Cloud (RELHIC). RELHICs provide exceptionally clean laboratories for probing dark matter, free from the baryonic complexities associated with star formation and feedback. We show that the observed hydrogen column density profile of Cloud-9 is consistent with a gas cloud embedded in either a cuspy halo predicted by the standard cold dark matter (CDM) model or a cored halo produced by self-interacting dark matter (SIDM). In both cases, the halo must have an unusually diffuse central density. The best-fitting CDM halo lies around $7σ$ below the cosmological concentration--mass relation, whereas SIDM core-forming halos reduce the tension to only around $3σ$. We further identify Cloud-9 analogs in the Concerto suite of cosmological zoom-in simulations with velocity-dependent SIDM, demonstrating that RELHICs provide a promising new probe of dark matter self-interactions.

AI.tldr: The paper analyzes Cloud-9, a gas-rich hydrogen cloud without an optical counterpart discovered near M94 by the Five-hundred-meter Aperture Spherical Telescope, as a Reionization Limited HI Cloud (RELHIC). The authors show its hydrogen column density profile is consistent with both cuspy CDM halos and cored SIDM halos, though both require unusually diffuse central densities. The CDM fit is ~7σ below the cosmological concentration-mass relation, while SIDM core-forming halos reduce this tension to ~3σ. Using the Concerto cosmological zoom-in simulation suite with velocity-dependent SIDM, the authors demonstrate RELHICs are a promising new probe of dark matter self-interactions.
AI.motivation: RELHICs provide exceptionally clean laboratories for probing dark matter properties because they lack optical counterparts and are free from the baryonic complexities associated with star formation and feedback. Cloud-9 represents a new opportunity to test dark matter models.
AI.method: The authors compare the observed hydrogen column density profile of Cloud-9 against predictions from both cuspy halos (standard CDM) and cored halos (SIDM). They quantify the statistical significance of each fit against the cosmological concentration-mass relation, and identify Cloud-9 analogs in the Concerto suite of cosmological zoom-in simulations with velocity-dependent SIDM.
AI.result: Both cuspy CDM and cored SIDM halos can reproduce the observed profile, but both require unusually diffuse central densities. The best-fitting CDM halo sits ~7σ below the concentration-mass relation, whereas SIDM core-forming halos reduce the tension to ~3σ. Cloud-9 analogs are found in the Concerto simulations, supporting the viability of the SIDM interpretation.
AI.conclusion: RELHICs such as Cloud-9 offer a promising new probe of dark matter self-interactions, and the data favor (though do not unambiguously require) SIDM over standard CDM in this case, warranting further investigation.

title: FAST Ultra-Deep Survey: the baryonic Tully-Fisher relation in FUDS0 field
comment: 21 pages, 15 figures, accepted for publication in ApJ
summary: The Baryonic Tully-Fisher relation (BTFR) is one of the tightest scaling relations for disk galaxies in the local Universe, and therefore is an important tool for studying the fomation and evolution of galaxies. However, the evolution of the BTFR over cosmic time is poorly understood due to the limited sample of HI galaxies beyond the local Universe, limitations of optically-derived rotation curves, and selection effects. In this work, we explore the BTFR at redshifts up to $z=0.42$ from galaxies detected in the pilot FAST Ultra-Deep Survey (FUDS) field, FUDS0. As found in previous work, we identify two components in the plane of baryonic mass versus rotational velocity, $C_{\rm BTFR}$ (tight) and $C_{\rm Outlier}$ (dispersed). A Gaussian mixture model is employed to recover the BTFR, yielding the best fit parameters for the slope $k=3.32_{-0.11}^{+0.12}$, zero point $b=10.07_{-0.03}^{+0.03}$, and intrinsic scatter $σ_{\rm BTFR}=0.036_{-0.009}^{+0.010}$. A random forest classifier is used to investigate the origin of the outlier component. We find that low signal significance and inaccurate inclinations are the key factors that contribute to the outlier population, indicating that observational effects are the dominant origin. Evolutionary trends are examined in three different redshift bins. Both the slope and zero point show consistency within 1-$σ$ uncertainty in the two low redshift bins, indicating no significant evolution. The indirectly inferred BTFR parameters from the $C_{\rm Outlier}$ component in the highest redshift bin aligns with the conclusion. The ongoing full FUDS survey will provide a larger sample to enable more accurate constraints on BTFR evolution.

AI.tldr: This paper explores the Baryonic Tully-Fisher Relation (BTFR) at redshifts up to z=0.42 using galaxies from the pilot FAST Ultra-Deep Survey (FUDS) field, finding no significant evolution in the BTFR slope and zero point across redshift bins, and identifying observational effects (low signal significance and inaccurate inclinations) as the dominant origin of the outlier population.
AI.motivation: The BTFR is a crucial scaling relation for disk galaxies and an important tool for studying galaxy formation and evolution, yet its evolution over cosmic time is poorly understood due to limited HI galaxy samples at higher redshifts, limitations of optically-derived rotation curves, and selection effects. This work aims to constrain the BTFR evolution beyond the local Universe.
AI.method: The authors analyze galaxies from the pilot FUDS field (FUDS0) up to z=0.42. They identify two components in the baryonic mass versus rotational velocity plane: a tight component (C_BTFR) and a dispersed component (C_Outlier). A Gaussian mixture model is used to recover the BTFR, yielding slope k=3.32, zero point b=10.07, and intrinsic scatter σ=0.036. A random forest classifier is employed to investigate the origin of the outlier component, and evolutionary trends are examined across three redshift bins.
AI.result: The BTFR fit yields slope k=3.32^{+0.12}_{-0.11}, zero point b=10.07±0.03, and intrinsic scatter σ_BTFR=0.036. The random forest classifier shows that low signal significance and inaccurate inclinations are the key contributors to the outlier population, indicating observational effects dominate. The slope and zero point are consistent within 1-σ in the two low redshift bins, showing no significant evolution, and the highest redshift bin's indirectly inferred parameters from the outlier component align with this conclusion.
AI.conclusion: The BTFR shows no significant evolution up to z=0.42, and the outlier component in the BTFR plane is primarily driven by observational effects rather than intrinsic galaxy properties. The full FUDS survey will enable more accurate constraints on BTFR evolution with a larger sample.

title: Detection and Properties of Lyman Break Galaxies at $1.6 \leq z \leq 3.0$ in GOODS-North
comment: 8 pages, 5 figures, Presented at BINA2025 conference, Accepted in Bulletin of Liège Royal Society of Sciences
summary: Lyman Break Galaxies (LBGs) are actively star-forming galaxies identified through their characteristic rest-frame ultraviolet spectral break, making them powerful probes of galaxy evolution across cosmic time. We present a search for LBGs at redshifts $1.6 \leq z \leq 3.0$ in the GOODS-North field using the dropout technique combined with color selection from the 3D-HST data. We utilize two selection criteria to identify LBG candidates at $z \sim 2.1$ and $z \sim 2.7$ via F275W- and F336W-dropouts, yielding 192 and 135 newly identified LBG candidates in the redshift ranges $1.6 \leq z \leq 2.3$ and $2.3 < z \leq 3.0$, respectively. We estimate the physical properties of the LBG candidates, including stellar age, stellar mass, and star formation rate (SFR), using spectral energy distribution (SED) fitting. Morphological analysis shows that the majority of galaxies in our sample exhibit disc-like structures. Overall, the results indicate that these LBGs are low- to intermediate-mass compact galaxies with effective half-light radii of approximately 3.5 kpc.

AI.tldr: This paper presents a search for Lyman Break Galaxies at redshifts 1.6 ≤ z ≤ 3.0 in the GOODS-North field using dropout and color selection from 3D-HST data, identifying 192 candidates at z~2.1 and 135 at z~2.7. The galaxies are characterized as low- to intermediate-mass compact disc-like galaxies with effective half-light radii of ~3.5 kpc, with physical properties derived from SED fitting.
AI.motivation: Lyman Break Galaxies are important probes of galaxy evolution across cosmic time, and identifying a large sample of LBGs at intermediate redshifts (1.6 ≤ z ≤ 3.0) enables better understanding of galaxy formation and evolution during this critical epoch.
AI.method: The authors use the dropout technique combined with color selection from 3D-HST data in the GOODS-North field. Two selection criteria are applied to identify LBG candidates at z~2.1 (F275W-dropouts) and z~2.7 (F336W-dropouts). Physical properties (stellar age, stellar mass, SFR) are estimated via SED fitting, and morphological analysis is performed.
AI.result: The search yields 192 LBG candidates in the redshift range 1.6 ≤ z ≤ 2.3 and 135 candidates in 2.3 < z ≤ 3.0. The galaxies are predominantly disc-like structures, low- to intermediate-mass and compact, with effective half-light radii of approximately 3.5 kpc.
AI.conclusion: The newly identified LBG sample at z~2.1 and z~2.7 comprises compact, disc-dominated, low- to intermediate-mass star-forming galaxies, expanding the known LBG population at these redshifts and offering new constraints on galaxy evolution.

title: The two faces of tides: gravitational instability during galaxy mergers
comment: 13 pages, 11 figures, 1 table
summary: Gravitational instability is a fundamental mechanism driving collapse of interstellar gas, yet in dynamically evolving environments such as galaxy mergers, external tidal fields can significantly alter the conditions for collapse. In this work, we develop an analytical framework to investigate how the tidal field of a companion galaxy modifies the classical Jeans instability by incorporating its anisotropic and time-dependent nature into the dispersion relation. We find that the tidal field introduces a critical angle between the cloud's position vector and the merger axis, $θ_c \approx 54.7^\circ$, separating disruptive and compressive regimes of the radial tidal component. Disruptive tides suppress instability by increasing the characteristic length scale and restricting the range of unstable modes, whereas compressive tides enhance collapse by extending the unstable spectrum and increasing the growth rate of perturbations. The impact of tidal fields depends sensitively on gas density, being significant in diffuse media but negligible in dense molecular environments where the classical Jeans limit is recovered. All tidal effects peak near pericentric passage due to the strong dependence on galaxy separation. Since the free-fall time of diffuse gas is comparable to the duration of the close passage, tidally assisted collapse in the diffuse medium lags pericentre by roughly a free-fall time, whereas dense gas responds essentially instantaneously. These results demonstrate that companion-induced tidal fields play a key role in regulating the scale and efficiency of gravitational instability of diffuse interstellar gas in galaxy mergers. The code underlying this work is publicly available.

AI.tldr: This work develops an analytical framework showing how companion galaxy tidal fields modify classical Jeans instability in mergers, revealing a critical angle (~54.7°) separating disruptive and compressive tidal regimes, with effects significant in diffuse gas but negligible in dense media, peaking near pericenter.
AI.motivation: Gravitational instability drives interstellar gas collapse, but in dynamically evolving environments like galaxy mergers, external tidal fields from companion galaxies can significantly alter collapse conditions, yet their anisotropic and time-dependent nature has not been incorporated into the classical Jeans instability analysis.
AI.method: The authors develop an analytical framework that incorporates the anisotropic and time-dependent tidal field of a companion galaxy into the dispersion relation, extending the classical Jeans analysis to merger environments.
AI.result: The tidal field introduces a critical angle θ_c ≈ 54.7° between the cloud's position vector and merger axis. Disruptive tides suppress instability by increasing characteristic length scale and restricting unstable modes, while compressive tides enhance collapse by extending the unstable spectrum and increasing growth rates. Effects depend sensitively on gas density—significant in diffuse media, negligible in dense environments—and peak near pericentric passage. Diffuse gas lags pericenter by ~one free-fall time while dense gas responds instantaneously.
AI.conclusion: Companion-induced tidal fields play a key role in regulating the scale and efficiency of gravitational instability of diffuse interstellar gas in galaxy mergers, with code available publicly.

title: MIGHTEE-HI: Environmental effects of cosmic filaments on extragalactic HI detections in the COSMOS and XMM-LSS fields
comment: 16 pages, 8 figures, submitted to MNRAS
summary: Cosmic filaments have been recognised as influencing galaxy evolution, but their connection to galactic cold gas reservoirs is elusive, particularly at low redshifts. We investigate the influence of filaments on neutral hydrogen (HI) detections in galaxies at $0.02<z<0.09$, using the MeerKAT International GHz Tiered Extragalactic Exploration (MIGHTEE) survey in the COSMOS and XMM-LSS fields. We measure the fraction of optical galaxies from the Dark Energy Spectroscopic Instrument (DESI) Survey detected in HI emission as a function of stellar mass, morphology, local density, and the distance to the nearest filament. We find that galaxies closer to filaments have higher stellar masses, higher local densities, and a larger early-type fraction, all of which affect the HI detection. After controlling for these dependencies, filaments have measurable effects on HI detection. Late-type galaxies in low-local density environments show reduced HI detection fractions close to filaments across all stellar mass ranges, suggesting potential gas depletion through ram pressure stripping and cosmic web detachment. Massive early-type galaxies show an enhanced HI detection fraction in filaments compared to the voids, suggesting possible gas replenishment through filamentary accretion or gas-rich mergers. Our results suggest that cosmic filaments influence galactic HI gas reservoirs through various competing processes, whose relative importance varies with stellar mass and local density.

AI.tldr: This paper investigates how cosmic filaments affect neutral hydrogen (HI) gas reservoirs in galaxies at low redshift (0.02<z<0.09) using MIGHTEE and DESI survey data. After controlling for stellar mass, morphology, and local density, filaments measurably influence HI detection: late-type galaxies in low-density environments show reduced HI near filaments (gas depletion via ram pressure stripping/cosmic web detachment), while massive early-type galaxies show enhanced HI in filaments (gas replenishment via accretion or mergers).
AI.motivation: Cosmic filaments are known to influence galaxy evolution, but their connection to galactic cold gas (HI) reservoirs remains poorly understood, especially at low redshifts. This work aims to quantify how proximity to cosmic filaments affects HI detections in galaxies.
AI.method: The study uses MIGHTEE survey HI data in the COSMOS and XMM-LSS fields combined with DESI optical galaxy catalog. It measures the HI detection fraction as a function of stellar mass, morphology, local density, and distance to the nearest filament, while controlling for confounding dependencies among these parameters.
AI.result: Galaxies closer to filaments tend to have higher stellar masses, higher local densities, and larger early-type fractions. After controlling for these, filaments produce measurable effects: reduced HI detection in late-type, low-density galaxies near filaments (gas depletion), and enhanced HI detection in massive early-type galaxies in filaments (gas replenishment).
AI.conclusion: Cosmic filaments influence galactic HI gas reservoirs through multiple competing processes whose relative importance depends on stellar mass and local density, including gas depletion (ram pressure stripping, cosmic web detachment) and gas replenishment (filamentary accretion, gas-rich mergers).

title: The Roche-Lobe Radius in Newtonian and Non-Newtonian Gravity
comment: Accepted for publication in Astrophysics and Space Science
summary: In this paper, we extend the standard calculation of the Roche lobe from the Newtonian potential to non-Newtonian models, specifically Yukawa-type and power-law potentials. These models are significant because they arise from unification theories, such as those involving extra dimensions or scalar-tensor gravity. Furthermore, we develop fitting formulas for the equivalent volume radius R_L under these potentials, analogous to $Eggleton s$ formula for the Newtonian case. We calibrate the fitting formulas of the non-Newtonian potentials with their corresponding numerical solutions.

AI.tldr: The paper extends Roche lobe calculations from Newtonian gravity to non-Newtonian potentials (Yukawa-type and power-law), and develops calibrated fitting formulas for the equivalent volume radius under these potentials, analogous to Eggleton's Newtonian formula.
AI.motivation: Roche lobe calculations are fundamental in binary systems, but standard formulations assume Newtonian gravity. Non-Newtonian potentials arising from unification theories (extra dimensions, scalar-tensor gravity) become relevant in certain astrophysical contexts, so extending Roche lobe calculations to these potentials is necessary.
AI.method: The authors extend the standard Roche lobe calculation to Yukawa-type and power-law potentials. They develop fitting formulas for the equivalent volume radius under these non-Newtonian potentials, analogous to Eggleton's formula, and calibrate these fitting formulas against corresponding numerical solutions.
AI.result: The paper produces fitting formulas for the equivalent volume radius under Yukawa-type and power-law potentials, calibrated to numerical solutions, extending the standard Newtonian Roche lobe formalism.
AI.conclusion: The work provides practical analytical tools for computing Roche lobes in non-Newtonian gravity models, which is significant for studying binary systems in the context of unification theories involving extra dimensions or scalar-tensor gravity.
